raw_text:
The objective of this research is to identify and explain the persistent completion-time differences between sites using the same nominal work process through measurable factors. We'll focus on understanding the observable behaviors that contribute to these differences and the impact of these factors on workforce performance and productivity.

Assumptions
Assuming that completion times vary among similar sites due to differences in measurable factors such as workload management, skill level, worker behavior, and equipment usage.

Research design
A comparative case study approach will be used, with an emphasis on standardizing the nominal work process. The research will involve a cross-case analysis of a set of organization that use similar work processes but show variability in completion times. We will collect data through quantitative and qualitative methods, including surveys, observations, and interviews, across different time periods. We will use statistical and qualitative analyses to identify patterns and causal relationships.

Data or evidence needed
- Quantitative data on completion times and workload for each site
- Qualitative observations of worker behavior, skill level, and equipment usage
- Interview transcripts and survey responses detailing work processes, resource allocation, and employee perceptions

Measurement
1. Workload metrics: Total number of tasks completed, task complexity, and task prioritization
2. Skill level metrics: Average years of experience, literacy levels, and educational background
3. Worker behavior metrics: Time spent on non-work tasks, collaboration frequency, and work rate
4. Equipment usage metrics: types of equipment used, equipment capacity, and repair records

Analysis
We will first describe the completion-time differences and potential factors contributing to them using statistical and qualitative analysis. We'll then use regression analysis and content analysis to identify and test the relationship between the measurable factors and completion times. This analysis will help us tease out the most significant factors and their relative impacts on completion times.

Decision / stopping rule
The decision to stop will be based on reaching a saturation point in the data (i.e., when no new patterns or insights can be identified), or when the predetermined time or resources constraints have been reached.

Limitations
The research is limited by the selection of the participating organizations, which might not represent the entire population. Additionally, the data may not be fully comprehensive or may be subject to bias, including recall bias in interviews and surveys. Lastly, external factors such as organizational culture and environmental conditions may also play a role in completion times but are outside the scope of this study. Nonetheless, we will exercise caution to minimize the impact of these limitations on our findings.
